analyses.title: Towards identifying unresolved discussions in student online forums
analyses.research_question: Can message-level forum speech acts and the resulting thread-level discourse structures be used to identify student discussions containing unanswered questions, confusion, or unresolved issues?
analyses.methodology: The authors define forum speech acts (F-SAs) describing roles of individual messages in threaded student Q&A discussions, including questions, issue raising, and answers. They then construct thread-level discourse structures from those labels, including whether a question receives an answer, and use these structures as features for classifying unresolved discussions. The accessible abstract reports evaluation of several discussion-classification problems but does not expose enough methodological detail to reconstruct the corpus, annotation procedure, classifier configurations, or individual task results.

key_findings.finding: The proposed representation explicitly records whether a question in a discussion thread was followed by an answer, making unanswered-question status a modeled discourse property rather than merely a lexical property of individual messages.
Forum speech acts distinguish communicative roles such as questions, issue raising, and answers before thread-level classification is performed.

The approach uses combinations of message-level speech acts to represent larger discourse structures and then uses those structures to identify discussions with unresolved issues or unanswered questions.
The reported discussion-thread classifiers achieved accuracies ranging from 0.79 to 0.87 across several classification problems.
The accessible abstract does not establish that the method distinguishes a fully answered question from a partially answered multi-proposition question.
The accessible abstract does not report proposition-level many-to-many alignment for threads containing multiple questions and multiple answers.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible from the source read, so corpus size, annotation reliability, feature details, classifier baselines, and per-task metrics could not be verified.
The accessible evidence models answer presence at the question or discussion-structure level but does not demonstrate explicit partial-answer labels.
The accessible evidence does not show how multiple questions in one message or thread are individually aligned to replies.
The accessible evidence does not establish whether unanswered subquestions inside an otherwise answered message are represented separately.
No public code or dataset release could be verified from the source read.
raw_claims: The work targets automatic identification of student discussions containing unresolved issues or unanswered questions.
Individual forum messages are first assigned forum speech-act roles.
Question, issue-raising, and answer are examples of the speech-act roles used by the system.
Thread-level discourse structures are constructed from the speech-act sequence and relationships.
Whether a question has received an answer is one of the discourse properties used by the approach.
The resulting discourse structures are used to classify discussions rather than relying only on isolated message content.
The reported classifiers obtain accuracies between 0.79 and 0.87 on several discussion-classification tasks.
The accessible abstract does not describe an explicit distinction between partial and complete answers.
The accessible abstract does not report proposition-level alignment within messages containing several questions.

analyses.title: Discourse parsing for multi-party chat dialogues
analyses.research_question: How can full discourse attachment and relation structure be parsed in multi-party chat when dialogues contain concurrent threads, crossing dependencies, multiple antecedents, and other non-tree structures?
analyses.methodology: The authors use the STAC Settlers of Catan chat corpus annotated with Segmented Discourse Representation Theory structures and transform its hypergraph-style annotations into EDU-level dependency structures for parsing. They train regularized maximum-entropy models over pairs of elementary discourse units using positional, lexical, syntactic, and dialogue-act features, with separate treatment of intra-turn and inter-turn dependencies under a forward inter-turn constraint. Local probabilities are supplied to several decoders, including Last, local classification, and a Maximum Spanning Tree decoder; the best configuration is selected by ten-fold cross-validation on training data and evaluated on a held-out test portion. The full corpus statistics reported are 1,091 dialogues, 10,677 EDUs, and 11,348 discourse relations, with 123 dialogues, 1,132 EDUs, and 1,190 relations in the test set.

key_findings.finding: The corpus contains genuine many-to-many discourse alignment: one question can receive several answer attachments, and a later acknowledgment can itself attach to several preceding answers.
key_findings.section: 2 What’s so special about multi party dialogue?

key_findings.finding: Non-tree discourse structures account for at least 9% of links in the corpus, so a representation forcing exactly one tree parent cannot faithfully represent all observed reply and antecedent relations.
key_findings.section: 2 What’s so special about multi party dialogue?

key_findings.finding: Complex Discourse Units can combine several EDUs into a single discourse antecedent; the paper gives an example where two utterances jointly form the antecedent of a conditional relation and notes that some CDUs encompass an entire question-answering session.
key_findings.section: 2 What’s so special about multi party dialogue?

key_findings.finding: Concurrent conversation threads create crossing dependencies, including replies or comments directed to material from another active thread, which makes simple adjacency-based reply alignment inadequate.
key_findings.section: 2 What’s so special about multi party dialogue?

key_findings.finding: The best global parser achieved directed attachment F1 of 0.671, undirected attachment F1 of 0.680, and fully labeled structure F1 of 0.516 on the held-out test corpus.
The Last baseline obtained attachment F1 of 0.584 and fully labeled F1 of 0.391, while the undecoded local classifier obtained directed attachment F1 of 0.541 and fully labeled F1 of 0.446.

Although MST decoding performed best among the tested global configurations, the authors estimate that a tree decoder cannot exceed 91% attachment performance even with a perfect local model because the gold discourse structures contain non-tree links.

The paper provides evidence about attachment structure and Question-Answer-Pair relations but does not introduce an explicit label for whether an answer completely versus partially resolves the semantic propositions in a question.

limitations: The parser converts SDRT hypergraphs to dependency structures by replacing Complex Discourse Units with recursive EDU heads, losing explicit CDU membership information during parsing.
The local model predicts pairwise EDU relations rather than learning the full discourse graph directly.
Maximum Spanning Tree decoding cannot represent all gold non-tree structures and has an acknowledged theoretical ceiling on this corpus.
The study uses task-oriented Settlers of Catan chat, so transfer to email, enterprise dialogue, or other conversational domains is not demonstrated.
The model does not explicitly score semantic completeness of an answer or identify which propositions within a multi-proposition question remain unanswered.
Attachment prediction and relation labeling are treated as separate prediction problems.
The paper notes that a general reliable method for predicting CDU membership edges was not available.
Cross-corpus comparisons to monologue parsers are explicitly described by the authors as difficult.
raw_claims: Multi-party chat can contain several simultaneous conversational threads.
A single question in the corpus can have several distinct responses attached to it.
One later acknowledgment can attach to the contents of several preceding responses.
Non-tree structures account for at least nine percent of discourse links in the corpus.
Crossing dependencies occur because participants may respond across concurrently active threads.
SDRT Complex Discourse Units allow several elementary units to function together as one discourse constituent.
Some Complex Discourse Units encompass an entire question-answering sequence.
The annotated corpus contains 1,091 dialogues, 10,677 elementary discourse units, and 11,348 discourse relations.
The held-out test set contains 123 dialogues, 1,132 EDUs, and 1,190 relations.
Inter-annotator agreement previously reported for the annotations was kappa 0.72 for attachment structure and 0.58 for relation labeling.
The best global model combines Last for intra-turn structure with MST-based global decoding under the turn constraint.
The best reported global result is 0.680 undirected attachment F1, 0.671 directed attachment F1, and 0.516 fully labeled F1.
Tree-based MST decoding cannot reproduce every gold graph because some discourse units participate in non-tree attachment configurations.
The paper does not provide an explicit complete-answer versus partial-answer semantic distinction.
